abstract: As LLM agents are deployed in long-horizon sessions, context accumulation drives up inference costs. Existing approaches utilize text pruning or dynamic memory eviction to minimize token footprints; however, their unconstrained sequence mutations alter layouts, introducing prefix mismatches and cache invalidation. This reveals a critical trade-off between text sparsity and prompt cache continuity. To address this, we present TokenPilot, a dual-granularity context management framework. Globally, Ingestion-Aware Compaction acts as a framework harness to stabilize prompt prefixes and eliminate open-world environmental noise at the ingestion gate. Locally, Lifecycle-Aware Eviction monitors the ongoing residual utility of context segments, enforcing a conservative batch-turn schedule to offload content segments only when task relevance expires. Experiments on PinchBench and Claw-Eval under both isolated and continuous modes demonstrate that TokenPilot reduces costs by 61% and 56% in isolated mode, and 61% and 87% in continuous mode, while maintaining competitive performance compared to prior systems.

sections.body:
The section argues that text pruning, dynamic memory eviction and summarization shorten context but change prompt layouts. These changes cause prefix mismatches and cache invalidation, which creates a trade-off between text sparsity and prompt cache continuity. Figure 1 is cited to illustrate this.

The proposed TokenPilot has two parts:
- **Ingestion-Aware Compaction** stabilizes the prompt prefix from the first turn by replacing volatile fields with placeholders, moving tool definitions downstream, and stripping noise from tool responses.
- **Lifecycle-Aware Eviction** offloads a context segment only when its task relevance expires.

The stated evidence is cost reduction of 61% and 56% in isolated mode and 61% and 87% in continuous mode, with competitive performance.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Text pruning cuts tokens but mutates prompt layouts and breaks cache reuse, so TokenPilot pairs ingestion stabilization with lifecycle eviction.

sections.body:
The section defines the setting. An agent processes a sequence of tasks. In isolated mode the context is reset at each task boundary. In continuous mode the history persists across the whole sequence.

A context management framework maps the raw history to an optimized context. The stated objective is to maximize context utility divided by serving cost. Serving cost counts cache-hit tokens at a discounted rate, where the rate is much less than one, and cache-miss tokens at full pre-fill cost. Hit and miss tokens must sum to the context length. The section reports no experimental results.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Serving cost is modeled as discounted cache-hit tokens plus full-cost miss tokens across isolated and continuous task modes.

sections.body:
TokenPilot has two components.
- **Ingestion-Aware Compaction** applies a canonicalization operator that substitutes volatile runtime markers with static placeholders. It also reduces environmental tool messages at the ingestion gate. Full content is kept in an artifact registry and can be recalled.
- **Lifecycle-Aware Eviction** tracks each segment through the states active, completed and evictable. A segment becomes evictable only when its residual utility is empty, and the eviction pass runs once per batch of B turns.

An estimator model, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, classifies segments zero-shot. The section states its cost across the continuous PinchBench stream is less than USD 0.03.
sections.heading: TokenPilot
sections.headline: The framework stabilizes prompt prefixes at ingestion and evicts context segments only after their residual utility expires, in batches of turns.

sections.body:
Experiments use PinchBench and Claw-Eval in isolated and continuous modes. Cache-hit and cache-miss token counts come from provider metadata fields. Baselines include LLMLingua-2, SelectiveContext, Keep-Last-N, Summary, LCM, Pichay, MemoBrain, AgentSwing and MemOS, all run on GPT-5.4-mini.

Table 2 reports Claw-Eval isolated mode: TokenPilot scores 63.1 at a cost of USD 2.27, against Vanilla at 64.5 and USD 5.16. Table 7 compares retention signals on PinchBench. The residual-utility estimator has the lowest cost, USD 4.69, on category-grouped streams. On mixed-category streams it is again the lowest-cost signal, at USD 5.25 against Recent-turn. Figures 3 to 7 show per-call context, cache hit rates, character savings, batch-size effects and a tool-call case study.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On Claw-Eval isolated mode, TokenPilot scores 63.1 at USD 2.27 cost, versus Vanilla's 64.5 at USD 5.16.

sections.body:
The related work groups prior methods into three lines.

- **Static content compression and abstraction** prunes or compresses text at ingestion, offloads session histories to external stores, and replaces trajectories with summaries, sub-goal graphs or knowledge graphs.
- **Dynamic and runtime scheduling** treats the context window as a resource, using demand paging, parallel routing, context isolation and virtual memory abstractions.
- **Multi-agent runtime scheduling** applies role-aware routing, experience caching or cross-context cache communication across agents.

The section does not report experimental comparisons.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work covers static text compression, passive memory retrieval and summarization, and runtime paging and scheduling of context.

sections.body:
The conclusion summarizes the paper. TokenPilot is presented as a dual-granularity framework that separates global ingestion-aware compaction from local lifecycle-aware eviction. The authors state that the framework stabilizes dynamic layouts and offloads context based on task-level residual utility.

The conclusion cites evaluations on PinchBench and Claw-Eval. It states that TokenPilot drastically cuts inference expenditures in isolated and continuous modes without sacrificing task effectiveness. It describes the framework as a foundation for long-horizon agent systems. No new numbers are given in this section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion states that TokenPilot cuts inference cost in both modes without sacrificing task effectiveness.

sections.body:
The limitations section states four constraints.

- The model-based estimator may misclassify segments when interaction patterns are highly ambiguous or sparse.
- The frequency threshold tau and batch size B may need tuning for each deployment and task distribution.
- The prefix stabilization component depends on backend prefix caching and gives no benefit to providers without it.
- Continuous evaluation groups same-category tasks. Heavily shuffled or heterogeneous streams may show lower prefix reuse because tool schemas keep changing.

The authors leave the last point for future work.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limits include estimator misclassification, tuning of threshold tau and batch size, dependence on prefix caching, and weaker reuse on shuffled streams.

sections.body:
The appendix covers the evaluation setup. PinchBench has 123 tasks in 11 categories. Claw-Eval's General group has 161 tasks.

Cost is computed from cache-hit tokens, cache-miss tokens and output tokens. The stated prices follow GPT-5.4-mini tiers: USD 0.075 per million hit tokens, USD 0.75 per million miss tokens and USD 4.50 per million output tokens.

It also documents baseline thresholds, reduction hyperparameters such as a 2200-character trigger, the batch window of 3, and estimator prompts. Table 9 and Table 10 give mixed-category PinchBench results, where prefix stabilization lowers cost for Vanilla from 21.16 to 17.09.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists benchmark statistics, cost formula and prices, baseline settings, hyperparameters, estimator prompts, and mixed-category results.
